newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus keeps falling despite weaker yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus keeps falling despite weaker yen.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus plunged by more than a third in the first half of this fiscal year despite a weaker yen, confirming that the contentious trade gap is still shrinking although at a slower pace.

The current account surplus -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- plunged 35.3 percent in the six months to September to 3.33 trillion yen compared with a year ago, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) said on Monday.

At Monday's exchange rate of around 112 yen to the dollar, the first-half current account surplus was equivalent to $29.7 billion. The surplus in merchandise trade alone in the six months decreased by 32.1 percent from the same period a year earlier to 4.16 trillion yen ($37 billion).
"Japan's trade surplus continues its declining trend... The weak yen is not causing any major effects," a MOF official told reporters.

The dollar's rise against the yen, from about 107 yen at the beginning of the fiscal year in April to about 111.5 yen at the end of September, was the main cause of the slowdown in the pace of the decrease in the surplus as it fuelled a rebound in exports and capped growth in imports, economists said.

The MOF also released data for September's current account surplus, which fell 35.6 percent from a year earlier to 727.4 billion yen ($6.49 billion). The September merchandise trade surplus slid 27.1 percent to 973.7 billion yen ($8.69 billion).

"The current account surplus in September was smaller than expected due to about a 1.5 times increase in the services trade deficit from a year ago," said Tetsuro Sawano, an economist at Nikko Research Centre.

"Excluding this factor, it is clear that the decline in the merchandise trade is slowing down. So the general trend of the current account surplus is that it will continue to fall but at a milder rate," Sawano said.

Jason James, a strategist at James Capel in Tokyo, said he expects the current account surplus in the second half of the fiscal year to decrease 25 percent from the same period a year earlier, which should be good news for the economy, although the drop will be milder than in the first half.
But some economists said there was a possibility of the surplus rising again next fiscal year, citing the rise in the customs-cleared trade surplus for the first 20 days of October.
"The drop in the surplus was sharp this past two to three years. There may be a situation where the surplus may rise slightly in reaction to this in the next year," Sawano said.

Hiroshi Suzuki, an economist at Norinchukin Research Institute, said the hike in Japan's consumption tax to five percent from current three percent next April would dampen domestic demand and cap imports.
Exports such as ships and cars will regain competitiveness from the weaker yen, he added. A drop in the yen makes Japanese products cheaper in terms of foreign currency.
But any rise in the trade surplus would be limited as the yen would likely start rising against the dollar if the surplus begins to expand, economists said.
The greater trend of Japanese companies moving their production overseas will not stop, though they may delay their plans depending on foreign exchange rates, they said.

Faced with the pressing need to protect their mighty export incomes, an increasing number of firms have shifted output to lower-cost economies at the expense of their domestic bases, a phenomenon known as the "hollowing out" of Japanese industry.
Recent informal surveys conducted by the Finance Ministry show companies are not planning to change the ratio of overseas and domestic output due to the weak yen, the MOF official said.
